plan.topic: Irkutsk suspected pneumonic plague case status decoder: what Russian authorities, WHO and CDC have actually said (as of Oct 7, 2026)
plan.angle: Three dated, attributed columns: confirmed, reported and still unknown. (1) Russian authorities, as reported by NBC and Reuters: the death is recorded as pneumonia of undetermined origin, and no plague was found in contacts. About 60% of roughly 200 contacts had been tested by Oct 6, finding 2 COVID and 2 rhinovirus cases. (2) WHO: the risk is rated moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia and very low for Europe. WHO is still asking for pathogen details, and its Director-General said WHO has sought details about a reported second illness, which is unverified. Say it once, attributed, without amplifying it. (3) CDC: no indication of a broader US threat. Then the depth. Why 'suspected' and 'confirmed' differ: how plague is confirmed in a lab (culture, PCR, reference-lab confirmation, per CDC and WHO). Why the case was first described as a typical respiratory infection, per WHO. What pneumonic plague is, in 60 seconds, and why it is the only form that passes between people. How about 200 contacts are monitored through the incubation window, with preventive antibiotics when clinicians advise it. Madagascar 2017 as a precedent, using WHO figures only. What would change the official picture. Respectful: don't lead with the worker's name, no photos, no blame. No lab-accident speculation and no stigmatising the region. Calm close plus the line 'if you're worried, talk to a health professional'. Re-check every status line at publish time and update the 'as of' date.
plan.working_title: Irkutsk Plague Case: What's Confirmed vs Reported (as of Oct 7, 2026)
plan.why: Our top-momentum topic (95). Many viewers still think plague was confirmed, and decoders are our most repeatable formula (128-view long-form). Each official update gives us a fresh 'as of' hook.

script.hook_pattern: Myth attack (answers 'was plague confirmed?' in the first 5 seconds) + open loop (the one lab result that would change the official picture, paid off in the final chapter)

scenes.narration: Was plague confirmed in Russia? As of October 7, 2026, no. Russian authorities initially recorded the death as pneumonia of undetermined origin, and testing is still underway.

visual.fact: As of Oct 7, 2026: initially recorded as pneumonia of undetermined origin; testing underway

scenes.retention_device: Myth attack: the search question answered in the first 5 seconds

scenes.narration: And among the roughly 200 people placed under observation, tests so far haven't found plague. That's the part a lot of posts are skipping.
scenes.on_screen_text: No plague found in tested contacts

visual.stock_query: group of people with clipboard check

scenes.retention_device: Concrete dated number backs the promise

scenes.narration: But 'not confirmed' isn't the same as 'ruled out'. And that gap is exactly where the confusion lives.
scenes.retention_device: But/therefore turn that creates tension

scenes.narration: So here's the plan. Three columns: what's confirmed, what's only reported, and what's still unknown. Each one with who said it, and when.
scenes.retention_device: Clear promise of what the viewer gets

scenes.narration: And stay to the end, because there's one specific lab result that would change the official picture overnight. I'll tell you exactly what it is, and what would make this story quietly end.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in 'What would change the picture'

scenes.narration: First, a respectful note. A person died here. We won't use the worker's name or photo, and we won't guess how they got sick. We'll stick to what agencies have said on the record.
scenes.retention_device: Trust signal before the evidence

scenes.narration: Column one: the Russian health authorities, as reported by NBC News on October 6.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card resets attention

scenes.narration: The death was initially recorded as pneumonia of undetermined origin. Not plague. Not 'probable plague'. Undetermined.
scenes.retention_device: Short punchy rhythm emphasises the exact wording

scenes.narration: Rospotrebnadzor also said it found no incidents involving the handling of dangerous microorganisms at the lab, and Russian authorities told WHO that no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk. That's their statement as of October 6; WHO is still awaiting confirmation of which germ caused the pneumonia.
scenes.on_screen_text: Russia: no lab handling incidents found (Oct 6)
scenes.retention_device: The key reported fact most headlines skip

scenes.narration: About 200 people who'd had contact with the patient were placed under observation. By October 6, around 60% of them had been tested.

visual.stock_query: progress bar over group of people

scenes.retention_device: Surprising specific stat

scenes.narration: Those tests didn't find plague. What they did find was ordinary: 2 COVID cases and 2 rhinovirus cases. Rhinovirus is one of the common cold viruses.

visual.stock_query: test tubes with friendly virus cartoons

scenes.retention_device: Unexpected detail that reframes the scare

scenes.narration: So two things are true at once. The contacts tested so far look clear of plague. And roughly 4 in 10 still hadn't been tested as of October 6.
scenes.retention_device: Nuance beat that keeps it honest

scenes.narration: Now here's where it gets interesting. The World Health Organization's language is more careful than the headlines, in both directions.
scenes.retention_device: 'Here's where it gets interesting' re-hook before column two

scenes.narration: Column two: WHO. On October 6, its spokesperson said WHO's initial assessment rates the risk as moderate to low for Irkutsk oblast, low for Russia as a whole, and very low for the WHO European Region.
scenes.retention_device: Named agency, concrete dated ratings

scenes.narration: Notice what's not on that list: 'high'. And notice that 'very low' isn't 'zero'. Risk ratings are a snapshot, and WHO updates them as evidence comes in.
scenes.retention_device: Question-style reframe keeps the viewer thinking

scenes.narration: WHO has also said it's still waiting for details on which pathogen caused the pneumonia. In plain English: the cause hasn't been publicly pinned down yet.
scenes.retention_device: Plants the 'unknown' column

scenes.narration: On October 6, WHO's Director-General posted that WHO had asked Russia about media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. No agency has confirmed that report, so we'll leave it there.
scenes.retention_device: Stated once, attributed, with an explicit hedge

scenes.narration: Column three: the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. CDC has said there's no indication of a broader threat to the United States.
scenes.on_screen_text: Column 3: CDC, no broader US threat

visual.quote: No indication of a broader threat to the United States
visual.attribution: CDC statement, as reported by NBC News (Oct 6)

scenes.retention_device: Third column completes the pattern

scenes.narration: So here's the scoreboard as of October 7. Confirmed: a death, initially recorded as pneumonia of undetermined origin. Reported by Russian authorities: no plague in tested contacts, and no incidents involving the handling of dangerous microorganisms at the lab. Unknown: which germ caused the pneumonia, with WHO still awaiting details.

items: Confirmed: a death, initially recorded as undetermined pneumonia
Reported: no plague in tested contacts; no lab handling incidents found (Russian authorities)
Unknown: which germ caused the pneumonia (WHO awaiting details)

scenes.retention_device: Mid-video summary that pays off the three-column promise

scenes.narration: Which raises an obvious question. If no authority has confirmed plague, what do words like 'suspected' and 'confirmed' actually mean? Let's climb the ladder.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer bridges into next chapter

scenes.narration: Think of it as a ladder. Health agencies don't jump straight from 'sick person' to 'confirmed plague'. There are rungs in between.
scenes.retention_device: Analogy chapter card

scenes.narration: Rung one is 'suspected'. Symptoms that fit, plus a possible exposure that makes doctors think of plague. It's a reason to act and test. It isn't a diagnosis.
scenes.retention_device: Step-by-step build

scenes.narration: Rung two is 'presumptive'. A faster test comes back positive, like PCR for the bacterium's genes, or a rapid antigen test. A strong clue, but still not final.
scenes.retention_device: Escalation to the next rung

scenes.narration: Rung three is 'confirmed'. Usually that means growing Yersinia pestis from a sample like blood or sputum, and identifying it, often at a reference laboratory.
scenes.retention_device: Top of the ladder, defines the key term

scenes.narration: And culture isn't instant. The bacterium grows slowly, so a definite answer can take days, not hours.
scenes.retention_device: Explains why updates feel slow

scenes.narration: Here's the part people forget. The ladder works in both directions. Testing can push a suspected case up to confirmed, or rule plague out completely.
scenes.retention_device: 'Here's the part people forget' re-hook

scenes.narration: So when you see 'suspected', read it correctly. It doesn't mean they're pretty sure. It means there was enough reason to check. In this case, the 'suspected plague' label first spread through media reports. Russian health authorities have not confirmed plague, and WHO says it is still looking into the cause.

visual.fact: Suspected = enough reason to test. Here, no health authority has confirmed plague (as of Oct 7).

scenes.retention_device: Myth-fact card on a belief viewers hold, then a twist that sets up the next chapter

scenes.narration: So why is everyone saying 'plague'? Two reasons: she worked at an institute that studies plague, and early media reports called it suspected pneumonic plague. WHO says its monitoring picked up those media reports on October 2 and it contacted Russian authorities the next day.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the 'why say plague?' question with a concrete, dated timeline

scenes.narration: According to WHO's spokesperson, Russian authorities said the illness first looked like a typical respiratory viral infection. That's true of many pneumonias, which is why symptoms alone can't tell you the cause.
scenes.retention_device: Reframes the detail calmly and opens the symptom explainer

scenes.narration: For reference, here's how CDC describes pneumonic plague: fever, headache and weakness, then a fast-developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucus.
scenes.retention_device: Practical list the viewer can use

scenes.narration: Early on, much of that overlaps with flu, COVID or an ordinary bacterial pneumonia. Telling them apart takes a lab test.
scenes.retention_device: Connects symptoms back to the ladder

scenes.narration: Which is why you need 60 seconds of plague basics. Because once you know how it spreads, the 200 contacts make total sense.
scenes.retention_device: Timed promise plus forward link to contacts chapter

scenes.narration: Plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis. In nature it circulates in rodents and their fleas.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a quick-fire format

scenes.narration: It comes in 3 forms. Bubonic affects the lymph nodes, usually after a flea bite. Septicemic is in the bloodstream. Pneumonic is in the lungs.
scenes.retention_device: Fast list keeps pace high

scenes.narration: And here's the key fact. Pneumonic plague is the only form known to pass from person to person, through respiratory droplets when a sick person coughs.
scenes.on_screen_text: Only pneumonic spreads person to person
scenes.retention_device: Key fact flagged as key

scenes.narration: It also takes close contact. A review of past outbreaks found most transmission happened among people near a patient late in the illness, often family members and caregivers.
scenes.retention_device: Micro-story from historical outbreaks

scenes.narration: That's very different from measles, which can linger in the air of a room. CDC's plague guidance defines close contact as within about 6 feet, or 2 meters, of a pneumonic plague patient.

visual.myth: Pneumonic plague floats through the air like measles
visual.fact: It spreads mainly by droplets at close range: ~6 ft / 2 m (CDC guidance)

scenes.retention_device: Named comparator (measles) corrects a common belief

scenes.narration: The same review found simple measures, like masks and keeping distance from coughing patients, helped break the chain.
scenes.retention_device: Reassuring payoff after the risk fact

scenes.narration: Timing matters too. CDC says pneumonic plague usually shows up 1 to 3 days after exposure. WHO notes it can be as short as 24 hours.
scenes.retention_device: Stat card that sets up the contact-tracing clock

scenes.narration: And it's treatable. WHO says recovery rates are high when plague is detected and treated in time, within 24 hours of symptoms starting.
scenes.retention_device: Calm, evidence-backed reassurance

scenes.narration: A CDC review of US cases from 1900 to 2012 found the share of patients who died fell from 66% in 1900 to 1941 to 16% from 1942 to 2012, as antibiotics arrived.
scenes.retention_device: Surprising before-vs-after stat

scenes.narration: Short incubation. Close-contact spread. A treatment that works best early. Put those 3 together, and you understand exactly why 200 people are being watched.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff that opens the next chapter

scenes.narration: Contact tracing for plague is a race against a short clock. Find everyone who was close to the patient, and check on them regularly, typically for about a week.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with stakes

scenes.narration: In practice, that's 4 steps.

items: Test and treat anyone who gets sick

scenes.retention_device: Numbered list for fast scanning

scenes.narration: CDC guidance says close contacts of a pneumonic plague patient can be given a 7-day course of preventive antibiotics, decided by clinicians for each person.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete number plus how it works

scenes.narration: That's a medical decision, not a DIY one. Please don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics. If you think you've been exposed, contact a doctor or your local health authority.
scenes.retention_device: Safety line keeps trust

scenes.narration: Why about a week? Because it covers the usual incubation for pneumonic plague. If a contact gets through that window without symptoms, the concern drops away.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, answered immediately

scenes.narration: So time is information. Every day that passes without plague among contacts is a quiet, meaningful piece of evidence.
scenes.retention_device: Reframe that sets up the 'what would change' payoff

scenes.narration: And remember those results: 2 COVID cases and 2 rhinovirus cases. A few ordinary respiratory viruses turning up when you test over 100 people isn't surprising.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to an earlier detail

scenes.narration: But does this approach actually work against a real plague outbreak? We have a big, recent test case. And it's far larger than anything reported in Irkutsk.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop before section change

scenes.narration: In August 2017, Madagascar had an unusual plague outbreak. Unusual because it spread in cities, and because most cases were pneumonic.
scenes.retention_device: Micro-story opener

scenes.narration: WHO counted 2,417 confirmed, probable and suspected cases from August to late November 2017, including 209 deaths.
scenes.retention_device: Big number for scale

scenes.narration: About 77% were clinically classified as pneumonic, the form that can spread between people, in crowded cities.
scenes.retention_device: Escalating stakes

scenes.narration: And notice the word 'suspected' again. Most of the pneumonic cases counted were probable or suspected; only a minority were confirmed by a lab.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the ladder: the same lesson in a real outbreak

scenes.narration: The response is the template you're seeing now. Trace contacts, follow them for about a week, offer preventive antibiotics, and treat anyone who gets sick quickly.
scenes.retention_device: Links the precedent to today

scenes.narration: WHO reported thousands of contacts traced and offered preventive antibiotics. By late November, it reported that case numbers were declining.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of 'does it work?' loop

scenes.narration: Keep the scale in mind. Thousands of cases there. Here, as of October 7, one death initially recorded as pneumonia of undetermined origin, and no plague found among tested contacts.

visual.myth: One reported case means a big outbreak is coming
visual.fact: As of Oct 7: plague not confirmed; no plague found in tested contacts; WHO rates Russia's risk low

scenes.retention_device: Contrast that reframes the headline

scenes.narration: Now, the promise from the start. The one result that would change the official picture is a lab-confirmed identification of Yersinia pestis from the patient's samples, announced by health authorities.
scenes.on_screen_text: The result that changes the picture
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: If that happens, expect the official wording to move from 'pneumonia of undetermined origin' to 'confirmed plague', and WHO could revisit its risk rating.
scenes.retention_device: Teaches viewer what to look for

scenes.narration: Other signals worth watching are on the list. Each one should come from an agency, on the record.

scenes.retention_device: Forward-looking list gives reason to return

scenes.narration: And what would make this story quietly end? Contacts finishing their monitoring window with no plague, and a final cause of death published by the authorities.
scenes.retention_device: Second half of the promised payoff

scenes.narration: One warning for the next few days. You'll see screenshots, 'leaked' documents and anonymous claims. Until an agency says it on the record, it's a rumour, not an update.
scenes.retention_device: Viewer empowerment beat

scenes.narration: That's why every status line here carries a date. This is accurate as of October 7, 2026, based on statements up to October 6. The description links to the sources, so you can check for anything newer.
scenes.retention_device: Transparency beat before the checklist

scenes.narration: Here's your 30-second checklist for reading any plague headline this week.
scenes.retention_device: Practical takeaway chapter

scenes.narration: Check the date. Look for WHO, CDC or the national health authority. Remember that suspected isn't confirmed. And remember plague is treatable when it's caught early.
scenes.retention_device: Recap list for retention and saves

scenes.narration: If you live in or visit places where plague occurs naturally, like parts of the western US, CDC's basics are about rodents and fleas: don't handle sick or dead animals, and use flea control on pets.
scenes.retention_device: Practical prevention for the viewer

scenes.narration: Most important: if you've had a possible exposure, or you get sudden fever with cough or chest pain after one, contact a doctor or your local health authority urgently.
scenes.retention_device: Urgent-care line

scenes.narration: If you're worried, talk to a health professional. For context, WHO rates the risk as low for Russia and very low for the WHO European Region, and CDC sees no indication of a broader US threat.

script.cta: This story could change at any time. Subscribe to InforMed and we'll decode each official update, dated and sourced, without the hype. Next: pneumonic, bubonic and septicemic plague compared, and why only one spreads between people. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

factcheck.summary: The core news claims check out against NBC News (Oct 6) and UN News. Those claims are: the death was initially recorded as pneumonia of undetermined origin; about 200 people are under observation; about 60% of contacts were tested; tests found 2 COVID and 2 rhinovirus cases and no plague; Rospotrebnadzor reported no lab handling incidents; WHO rates the risk moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia and very low for the European Region; WHO's monitoring picked up media reports on Oct 2 and it contacted Russia on Oct 3; and CDC sees no indication of a broader US threat. A fresh search on Oct 7 found no official confirmation of plague, so 'not confirmed' still stands. Tone, safety lines, how the person who died is treated, and the dated hedges all meet the guardrails. The Kugeler figures (66% → 16%) and the Madagascar figures (2,417 cases and 209 deaths; 77% pneumonic, which fits 1,854 of 2,417; 22% of pneumonic cases confirmed) hold up. One problem needs fixing: the diagnosis ladder (s22–s24) attributes PCR and rapid antigen tests as 'presumptive', culture as the main route to 'confirmed', and 'culture takes days' to a CDC page that doesn't say this. CDC's case definition actually lists F1 antibody or F1 antigen tests as presumptive, and culture isolation or a fourfold rise in antibodies as confirmed. The other issues are small attribution and source fixes: the incubation wording, the 2 m conversion, the measles claim with no source, the Tedros post URL and date, and some wording consistency.

issues.claim: Presumptive = a faster test comes back positive, like PCR for the bacterium's genes, or a rapid antigen test (src_cdc_dx, src_who_fs)
issues.problem: The cited CDC diagnosis page doesn't describe PCR or rapid antigen tests as 'presumptive'. CDC's plague case definition gives the presumptive lab criteria as raised antibodies to the F1 antigen, or F1 antigen detected in a sample. The WHO fact sheet mentions a rapid dipstick test but doesn't call it presumptive. The source doesn't support the line as written.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "Rung two is 'presumptive'. A lab test points to plague, for example detecting a plague protein called the F1 antigen, or a rapid dipstick test. A strong clue, but still not final." Change source_ids to ["src_cdc_casedef", "src_who_fs"] and add the source src_cdc_casedef: "Plague 1996 Case Definition", CDC NNDSS, https://ndc.services.cdc.gov/case-definitions/plague-1996/

issues.claim: Confirmed usually means growing Y. pestis from blood or sputum, often at a reference laboratory (src_cdc_dx)
issues.problem: CDC's case definition confirms plague in one of two ways: isolating Y. pestis from a clinical sample, or a fourfold or greater rise in antibody titre. The fetched CDC diagnosis page says blood cultures are sensitive, but it doesn't mention reference laboratories.
issues.fix: Narration: "Rung three is 'confirmed'. That means growing Yersinia pestis from a sample like blood or sputum and identifying it, or a clear rise in antibodies over time." Change source_ids to ["src_cdc_casedef", "src_cdc_dx"].

issues.claim: The bacterium grows slowly, so a definite answer can take days, not hours (src_cdc_dx)
issues.problem: The cited CDC page doesn't give a culture growth time, so the claim is presented as CDC's without CDC saying it.
issues.fix: Narration: "And confirmation isn't instant. Growing and identifying the bacterium, or waiting for antibody changes, takes time, which is why official answers can lag behind headlines." On-screen text: "Confirmation takes time". Change source_ids to ["src_cdc_casedef"].

issues.claim: CDC says pneumonic plague usually shows up 1 to 3 days after exposure (src_cdc_symp)
issues.problem: The cited CDC symptoms page says pneumonic plague can develop within as little as one day after exposure. It doesn't state a '1 to 3 days' range.
issues.fix: Narration: "Timing matters too. CDC says pneumonic plague can develop within as little as 1 day after exposure, and WHO notes incubation can be as short as 24 hours. Across all forms, WHO gives 1 to 7 days." On-screen text: "Can start within ~1 day". Stat card: stat_value "~1 day", stat_label "pneumonic plague can start this soon after exposure (CDC, WHO)".

issues.claim: CDC's plague guidance defines close contact as within about 6 feet, or 2 meters; measles can linger in the air of a room
issues.problem: MMWR 2021 says 'within 6 feet'. The '2 meters' is our own conversion, but the line presents it as CDC's. The measles claim has no source tagged.
issues.fix: Narration: "That's very different from measles, which can linger in the air of a room. CDC's plague guidance says person-to-person spread requires exposure within 6 feet, about 2 metres, of a pneumonic plague patient." On-screen text: "Close contact: within 6 ft (CDC)". Add the source src_cdc_measles: "Measles: How It Spreads", CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/measles/causes/index.html

issues.claim: On October 6, WHO's Director-General posted that WHO had asked Russia about media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause
issues.problem: The source URL points to the X profile, not to the post itself. The content of the post (WHO asking about media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause) is confirmed through search and through Forbes coverage on Oct 7, but we couldn't verify the posting date of Oct 6.
issues.fix: Change the URL to https://x.com/DrTedros/status/2107591815863968121 and the narration to: "WHO's Director-General has posted that WHO asked Russia about media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. No agency has confirmed that report, so we'll leave it there."

issues.claim: Rospotrebnadzor found no incidents involving the handling of dangerous microorganisms
issues.problem: NBC quotes Rospotrebnadzor as saying 'pathogenic microorganisms'. The paraphrase changes the agency's wording.
issues.fix: Replace 'dangerous microorganisms' with 'pathogenic microorganisms' in the s08b narration and the s18 narration. Change the s08b on-screen text to "Russia: no lab handling incidents found (reported Oct 6)".

issues.claim: WHO says recovery rates are high when plague is detected and treated in time, within 24 hours of symptoms starting
issues.problem: In the WHO fact sheet, the 'within 24 hours' recovery statement is about pneumonic plague. The script widens it to all plague.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean, legible single-focal-point designs with brand colors and readable text at phone size. #0 (\"NOT CONFIRMED\" + \"AS OF OCT 7\" + microscope) most directly pays off the exact title promise (\"What's Confirmed vs Suspected\"), creates a strong expectation-violation hook for viewers who assume it's confirmed, and matches the channel's top-performing format (dated status decoder, which hit 128 views in long-form data). #1 (\"~200\") is also strong and uses the proven big-number formula, but it answers a different question than the one in the title, creating a slight mismatch between headline and title promise. #2 (\"WHAT CAUSED IT?\") is a good mystery hook but risks nudging toward cause-of-death speculation, which sits closer to the guardrails against fear-bait/speculation, and is the weakest match to the title's confirmed/suspected framing. #0 best balances CTR, legibility, and title alignment without overstepping guardrails.

issues.fix:
Replace the description field with this plain text (real line breaks):

Irkutsk suspected plague case: confirmed? As of Oct 7, 2026, no. Not confirmed isn't the same as ruled out. Confirmed vs reported vs unknown, dated and sourced.

Russian authorities initially recorded the lab worker's death as pneumonia of undetermined origin and told WHO no plague case has been recorded in Irkutsk (Oct 6); WHO awaits pathogen details. By Oct 6, about 60% of roughly 200 contacts were tested: 2 COVID, 2 rhinovirus, 0 plague (NBC News). About 4 in 10 hadn't been tested yet. WHO initial assessment (Oct 6): risk moderate to low (Irkutsk), low (Russia), very low (WHO European Region). CDC: no indication of a broader US threat.

This is educational content, not medical advice. If you're worried, talk to a health professional. Worried about symptoms or possible exposure? Contact a doctor or your local health authority urgently.
